scenario: AITA for wanting my girlfriend to be less braggy about her work perks? She seems to forget that the way she lives isn't how most people live... | My girlfriend has a pretty sweet job. She doesn't have set hours; she just has to work 35 hours a week whenever is convenient for her and make it to her few meetings. She can work from the office or from home sometimes. She has a full benefits package despite being under what most people consider full time. A really nice retirement package too. And the company will pay everything for continued education. She does work she finds interesting (cutting edge robotics) and gets along well with her coworkers. She has a lot of PTO per year and her boss even lets the employees "earn up" more; if they work extra hours one week they can ask for the equivalent in PTO for later. Her team's managers buy them whatever they want for the office; they want a 500 dollar expresso maker, they get it. They want a type of fancy coffee, they get it. Nice furniture, done... They get paid well too; pretty middle of the road salary for robotics but she says the work life balance more than makes up for it. She'd rather have more time than be a top earner. And honestly a midrange robotics salary is still damn good. And anyway, For a while I thought "good for her" for having found something that she is happy with. But recently it's gotten frustrating because I think she forgets that this isn't how everyone lives. Like when we're out with my friends or just hanging out she'll talk about the nice stuff her managers bought for the office, about all the vacations she takes, about how she and her coworkers left the office in the middle of the day to see a movie then came back and just worked a little later. And yeah, it seems like she forgets that is no way a normal job. So last night we were at a party and she mentioned how she was going to tour a few new apartments Monday morning and afternoon, and one of the people at the party was like "don't you have work" and she said "yeah but I can set my own hours" And that just rubbed me the wrong way and I said that she needed to stop going on and on about her work perks, it was obnoxious and came off braggy. She was like "I was just explaining something" and I said it wasn't just this, it was everything. Most people don't live the life she lives." She said that I was coming off jealous and that it was a bad look. That she was where she was because she didn't settle for less; she studied and worked her ass off, and didn't let herself get too settled anywhere she was unfulfilled. And that instead of complaining, maybe I should ask myself what I'm feeling jealous of and what I need to do to get it. I told her she was missing the point; she'll always be around people who don't have what she does, and she could be a little more modest about it. She said I was the only one who seemed to have a problem with it, and stormed off... AITA for what I said?

prediction.raw: **YTA (1)** *Here's why, broken down clearly and compassionately:* ### 1️️ **Her "bragging" is likely just normal conversation** - She’s sharing factual details about her job (e.g., "I can set my own hours" in response to "Don’t you have work?"). **This isn’t bragging**— it’s a straightforward answer to a question. - People * naturally* talk about positive aspects of their lives (jobs, hobbies, achievements). If she’s proud of her hard-earned stability (which she * earned* through study and effort), that’s human. - **Key distinction**: Bragging implies * intentionally* making others feel inferior. Her tone and intent matter more than the content. If she’s not * sneering* or * dismissive* of others’ struggles, she’s just living her life. ### 2️️ **You’re projecting your own insecurities onto her** - You said: " she forgets that this isn’t how most people live." **But it’s not her job to constantly self-edit to accommodate your feelings**. - If * you* feel uncomfortable hearing about her job, that’s * your* emotion to unpack—not hers to fix. - Her response to you ("*Maybe I should ask myself what I’m feeling jealous of*") was spot-on. Your frustration likely stems from your own job dissatisfaction or comparisons, not her actions. - **Example**: If a friend wins the lottery, you wouldn’t expect them to * never* mention it because others can’t afford luxury. You’d either celebrate their good fortune or privately process your own feelings. ### 3️️ **Your public criticism was harsh and unfair** - Calling her "obnoxious" at a party for a factual statement ("I can set my own hours") was ** disproportionate**. - A better approach would be: - *Privately* say: "I’ve been feeling a bit insecure about my own job lately, and when we talk about yours, it’s hard for me. Can we talk about it later?" - *Instead of* public accusations that made her feel attacked. - **Why this matters**: AITA isn’t about whether her job is "unfair"— it’s about whether * your reaction* was reasonable. Yours wasn’t. ### 4️️ **"Most people don’t live this way" is true—but irrelevant** - Yes, her job is exceptional (many would * love* her flexibility and benefits). **But that doesn’t mean she should apologize for it**. - If she * never* talked about her job, * you* might feel she’s being distant or unauthentic. - **The real issue**: You’re asking her to shrink her happiness to make you feel better. **That’s not fair**. ### 💡 **What to do instead** - **Reflect on your own feelings**: Are you dissatisfied with your job? Stressed about finances? * Those* are the things to address (e.g., career coaching, therapy, or a job search). - **Talk to her privately**: "I’ve been feeling insecure about my work situation lately. When we talk about your job, it’s hard for me. Can we support each other through this?" - **Celebrate her wins**: If you’re truly happy for her, say so! "I’m so proud of you for finding something that works so well for you." - **Remember**: Her job isn’t a personal affront to you. It’s * her* life. **Final verdict**: You were the asshole for publicly shaming her for normal conversation. Her job is a privilege she earned, and it’s not her responsibility to downplay it to protect your feelings. Focus on your own path forward. 💛 *(P.S. If you’re struggling with your job, I’m here to help brainstorm solutions— no judgment.)*
